utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The late start today is due to a lot of things coming in just one or two minutes before we would have started. Mr. Josse, I think you had an opportunity to look at the original of some of the documents that were presented yesterday. When could we -- are you satisfied -- from what I saw, what seemed to be very badly legible was as a matter of fact the writing on the back side of the -- the other side of the document. Any comments on that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. I'm delighted that the originals have been brought into the courtroom, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know that the originals will not stay in this courtroom for practical reasons, because they belong in another courtroom at this moment, but good copies, yes, the originals --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are -- coincidentally, there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second. Could we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The issue I just raised is a translation issue about yesterday which should not have dealt with in private session. That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've received this translation dated the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As has my learned friend and we're grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Josse, I take it you also received a copy of a memo which was addressed by the Registry to this Chamber regarding the problems in calling -- in getting Mr. Bjelica in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have not seen that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's an urgent matter and I would like you to -- from what I remember, a copy was sent to the -- to the Defence and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It may be in our locker, Your Honour, which isn't checked as -- that regularly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart and I attended quite a lengthy meeting with the Registry. I suspect I know what most if not all of what it contains and I would obviously would like to see it and if it's a matter that Your Honour needs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's not in your locker we will take care that there will be a copy available to you so that you could pay urgent attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from that -- yes. Apart from that there are a few more matters, but -- yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday after I asked the witness about the issue of his sentence, he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Unilaterally raised the issue of his sentence having been commuted to a fine of 4.500 Deutschmarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I made an urgent inquiry at the Court's behest and my own behest because the documents I had been provided did not reflect such a commutation but I can inform the Court that we received -- I received just before I walked into court a copy of the commutation and there is a decision commuting the sentence from a three-month sentence to a fine of 4.500 Deutschmarks. I have both the original and a translation which I will file with the Court as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, you have already received a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I haven't. My learned friend was good enough to tell me about it and allowed me to scan the document and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's good to tell the witness that you received a copy of this and if you do that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so he's -- that he -- there's no reason to be nervous about us not knowing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I intended to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there seem to be no any urgent procedural matters at this moment, I'd like to ask Madam Usher to call the witness back to court. Yes. Perhaps I had one thing, a number, P1124, was attributed to a document and later withdrawn. So this number will now be given to the next exhibit the Prosecution would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Maricic. Please be seated. I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Harmon, you're not yet at 60 per cent, but close to it. So I'd say, if you'd try to, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. That's I'll need, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, let me inform you before we begin the continued examination, you told me yesterday that your sentence, your gaol sentence had been commuted to a fine of 4.500 Deutschmarks. Following that revelation from you, I made an inquiry and have received a copy of a decision from the basic court in Brcko dated the 3rd of June, 2004, which decision does indeed reflect that your sentence was commuted. I have it, both an English translation and a B/C/S original of this. I will file a copy of this with the Court so you can be assured that the record is perfectly clear on the disposition of your case. Mr. Maricic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we pass out the next exhibit, please, and this is not an exhibit that's found in the binders but will need a new number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would that then be P1124?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, I want to return to a subject very, very briefly but a subject about which you testified yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That testimony, Your Honours, is found at page 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I asked you a question, Mr. Maricic, about the association of participants in the war in 1990, and your evidence was that there was no organisation by that name. Mr. Maricic, the Prosecution Exhibit 1124 is from the website of that organisation, and it says in the text as follows, and you were the president of that organisation so perhaps this will refresh your recollection: "The combatants' organisation of Republika Srpska was founded on 27th of June, 1993, under the name Republican Association of Participants in the War since 1990 of Republika Srpska, and as such it was registered with the Banja Luka Lower Court under number 2/93 of 9th August 1993. On 7th July 1997 pursuant to a decision by the Assembly, number 317/97 it changed its name to Combatants' Organisation of Republika Srpska and was registered under such name with the Banja Luka Lower Court, under number 31/97 of 18th July 1997." So I return to my question, Mr. Maricic. Why was the association named the Republican Association of Participants in the War since 1990?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the name is correct, but it's not true that it was established in 1990. Why somebody called it "since 1990," I don't know. I didn't take any part in the baptism of this organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware of it? First of all, when you said it was not founded in 1990, that's clear. That's what Mr. Harmon just read to you. But were you aware that it originally had this name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if you would have told us yesterday, "Mr. Harmon, that was the name the organisation originally had but we have changed it since then," that would have saved a lot of time and would have made matters immediately perfectly clear. So please try to assist this court, and that means you're called by the Defence and assist this Court in understanding as good as possible anything related to questions put to you. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Maricic, you have testified about when the war started in the municipality of Brcko. I come back to the question I asked you earlier. Why was this organisation named the republican association of participants in the war since 1990? What happened in 1990 that gave this group a desire to form an association related to the war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous evidence, I also told the truth, that it was set up in 1990 something, as it says here. And where the name comes from, I don't know. I didn't take any part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were the president of an organisation that bore the name of an association of participants in the war since 1990. Did you inquire why this was an association when the war had not started in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was this association in part for people who had prepared for war in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no explanation for that. I wouldn't even say that that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I can't go further on that subject, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question. Since when are you -- are you in that -- active in that organisation? Since when are you president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I became simultaneously president and active on the date of establishment in 1993, although I didn't stay president for very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In 1997 you were not president any more. Is that -- or were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I was president for maybe only a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And being president, on from the beginning, you never asked yourself why does this name refer to 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know. There must have been some reasons, but I never gave it any thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned it could have been '82 or '77 or '89? The name of an organisation is not an expression of what it is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't put it that way exactly, because in 1991, there were already multi-party elections and the democratic system was introduced. That's why it was 1990. If it had been earlier, I certainly would not have taken any part in that organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, we're going to turn to the topic that we ended your examination on yesterday, and that is the subject of paramilitaries. If I could have the document that is found in tab 7, the original document. Yesterday, as you recall, Mr. Maricic, there was an issue where the copy of the document in your language was illegible. I have obtained a copy of the original document which I'd like you to expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours -- no. It's not in respect of this exhibit. It's in respect of the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you inspect that document, please, Mr. Maricic? This document, Mr. Maricic, is issued by the War Presidency, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see at the lower right-hand side of this document type -- typewritten words, and can you read those words?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably mean the handwritten part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I mean the typewritten part in the lower right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "War Presidency of the Brcko municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this document, if you'd turn over the original, if you could turn over the original, there appear to be two names on the back of that document. One is Djordje Ristanic. We know who he is through your testimony. Pero Markovic. Who is Pero Markovic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pero Markovic was a Serb from Brcko who, when the multi-ethnic government was established, was president of the municipal government representing the Serb people in Brcko at the time when Mustafa Ramic was president in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What role or position did he hold in Brcko on the 7th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Pero Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not have a very important role. I don't remember. He later became a director of a bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this document was issued by the War Presidency, then, Mr. Maricic, to a volunteer by the name of Branislav Filipovic, one of the paramilitary volunteers who came to the Brcko municipality. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to another document, show you another document. This is a document, Mr. Maricic, that was issued a week later. This is found at tab 13 of the binder in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me inform the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, may I take it -- first of all, Mr. Registrar, a number had been assigned to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1127, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we now use only this colour copy version of this document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic -- the next document is found, Your Honours, at tab number 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I have substituted a redacted copy which I hope Your Honours have received, redacted copy of the B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document also based on a decision of the War Presidency. It's dated the 14th of May, 1992. It also is a pass, and it's issued to someone whose name you cannot see. And under the typewritten portion "War Presidency of the Brcko municipality," it is signed by Adolf. My first question for you, Mr. Maricic, do you know anybody who went by the name of Adolf who operated within the Brcko municipality in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Brcko municipality in 1992 when I was there, the only Adolf was Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Goran Jelisic was the commander of the Luka prison camp in 1992 for a period of time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- in fact, I got that information only after the war. I don't think he was warden. He was convicted here. He was a man who did whatever he pleased, and he did whatever he wanted with weapons, but I don't think he was officially warden of the Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in conjunction with this document I'd just like to refer Your Honours to some 92 bis evidence that was from Witness K214 that was submitted, and it also relates to an identical form of the document that I have presented now to this witness. Just for your reference; for Defence reference as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Witness, I want to refer your attention to the bottom portion of this document where it says, "100 per cent clean and vouched for." And again, signed by Adolf. What does that refer to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I did not hear this nickname or term, "Adolf." Only later did I hear that Goran Jelisic had this nickname. But from all my information, he was the only Adolf. As for clean, I have no idea what it is about. Goran at the time was in such a position that whomever he vouched for to be clean was considered clean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say whoever he vouched for is clean -- was considered clean, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The implication is that this was his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn to another topic. MR. HARMON I'm sorry, this needs a number. I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 13, Your Honours, will be P1129.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the document that is now found in tab 10, Mr. Maricic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One observation about tab 13. I appreciate there may be difficulties with this request. I'd like provenance of that in due course, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That request is never a problem. We will be glad to provide the provenance of that document to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this document I'd like to show you because -- Mr. Maricic, I'm sorry. Don't bother yourself with looking at that particular copy. That's illegible. I'd like to show you a more legible copy -- that the registrar could show you a more legible copy of this document. This document, Mr. Maricic, is a receipt handwritten at the right-hand corner is "13 May 1992." It's a receipt for the following temporary property -- I'm sorry, I'll read that again. "For the following military property received for temporary use by BP5055-19 Belgrade," and then it sayings in parentheses "(TO Brcko)." And then you'll see it is based on an order and it identifies a large amount of ordnance that was received by Branislav Filipovic. So this is a document, Mr. Maricic, again showing that there was a Brcko Territorial Defence on the 13th of May, 1992, and that Mr. Filipovic, who was a volunteer and has been identified as a volunteer, was cooperating with that organisation. May I have your comments on this particular document, Mr. Maricic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the approval for Mr. Filipovic to go to Belgrade, I'm not trying to defend anyone in this respect, but the president of the War Presidency had to sign. He had the seal, and he had to sign things submitted to him by others. Secondly, I told you that the Territorial Defence was established as the war started, but it didn't really amount to anything. Other people were involved that were organised under the umbrella of this TO. And I -- there was no TO commander even for those companies that existed. Other people had command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is correct, isn't it, Mr. Maricic, that the paramilitary units and members of those units cooperated both with the War Presidency and the Serbian TO in Brcko in May of 1992 and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not cooperate. They only issued orders. And this Djordje Ristanic, president of the War Presidency, was actually beaten up by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me continue then, Mr. Maricic, because the paramilitary units that came to Brcko, you've identified those paramilitary units. You've identified people as -- in the Arkan paramilitary force, Mauzer. You've identified Mr. Blagojevic, who you knew, and you've identified other members of paramilitaries that came in the beginning of the war in Brcko. Now, it's a fact, isn't it, Mr. Maricic, that Arkan was a well-known criminal before the start of the war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when did you --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war I had never even hard of Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The news started making the rounds as the war started in Brcko that there is such a man as Arkan and there is a group called Arkan's men. I cannot give you a precise time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you learn that he was a criminal and that his men were engaged in criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much later after the beginning of the war, much, much later, although the stories were already circulating after the war began that they are shipping goods out of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- let me just read something to you. This is found at Prosecution Exhibit 1090. This is an interview with Mr. Seselj, and I'll read a portion of that interview. Seselj and Mr. Poplasen were being interviewed publicly, and Mr. Seselj made the following remarks, and he said, "It is important to address the problem of crime. The worst problem of all, the Serbs in all Serbian countries, the main criminal activities have been going on during this war on the territory of the Republika Srpska and have been -- and the --" I lost my place, I'm sorry. "The main criminal activities of that have been going on in this war on the territory of the Republika Srpska and the Republika Srpska Krajina are linked to the regime in Serbia and the Serbian police. They are also linked to the counter-intelligence service of the army of Yugoslavia in which the communist members of the SK for Yugoslavia (and we have spoken about that before) are the leaders. For example, Zeljko Raznjatovic, "Arkan," a man of the Serbian UDBA who used to liquidate immigrants and rob banks in Western countries. In this war the press proclaimed him a Serbian hero, and he never had more than 2 to 3.000 men under his command. He said that he had liberated Bijeljina. That is not true, because they had only 29 men in Bijeljina. What did he do? He robbed Bijeljina? What did he do in Brcko? He robbed the Brcko port. He took away everything he could possibly take. The value of the goods he took away could be measured by millions of German marks. He could not have done it by himself. He shipped it with the permission of the Serbian police, Radmilo Bogdanovic, Sokolovic, Radovan Stojicic Badza, et cetera. That was sold on the black market and the money was shared." I won't read further. Now, that's correct what Mr. Seselj said about Arkan and what he did in Brcko, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is something illogical about that. Radovan Stojicic Badza, was not a Serb leader. He was a high official of the police of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Putting aside the names, Mr. Maricic, it is true what Seselj said about Arkan's looting of Brcko, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any comments on that. It's not only Arkan. There are many other people who shipped goods away. I was wounded at one point and I was absent for a long time, and it was all over by the time I came back, but a lot of that went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you -- let's return to the document, Mr. Maricic, that's found at tab 17. Mr. Maricic, this is a document we looked at yesterday at length. I want to refer you to page 7 in the Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I want to refer Your Honours to page 5 starting at the third paragraph in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, let me direct your attention the last two paragraphs. I'm going to read portions of that. You can follow along. This is the document that was prepared by Mr. Ristanic. "A special feature of the Brcko front is organised and individual crime in the form of looting. This has assumed such proportions that individuals have lost their lives and been wounded in their desire to steal. All stolen materials, vehicles, hi-fi's and other goods and valuables have passed through almost all checkpoints before ending up in Bijeljina. The good part of the war booty has crossed the Drina River and ended up in Serbia. The responsibility for this criminal offences must be passed. It is incomprehensible that an unregistered car or a car without licence plates can be driven around Bijeljina municipality." Then I'll end with that portion of the second paragraph and go to the next paragraph. "The result of the looting is that Brcko is now a devastated town. This has led to the fall of combat morale, significant demoralisation of the Brcko population and the absurdity of the whole war." And I want to go to the next paragraph, Mr. Maricic. "Certain formations have established their warehouses of looted goods in Brcko as well as Bijeljina, like, for example, the special unit in the duty-free zone. This unit has even produced its own seal so it can issue appropriate documentation. The command of this unit thinks it should have its own till, its own current account, and as said earlier that it should organise the public security station, the civilian political leadership, the military police and the entire command structure. It is important to mention that unit carry out an attack on the public security station (of which senior organs have already been informed). All of these activities have been accompanied by rapes, unauthorised interrogations, the issuing of dubious permits to leave town, probably for a hefty fee, and there are indications that the most drastic cases members of unknown formations have executed people." Now, Mr. Maricic, when you returned to Brcko after your rehabilitation from your serious wounds, you were aware of this weren't you? You were aware of the extensive nature of the looting that had taken place in Brcko, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything precisely, but in that war the same was done by all sides, including looting. As for Brcko, I said before and I can say it again, I don't know who had command. In that situation, there were certain individuals and groups who took advantage of that chaos and looted. But I didn't want to get involved in that, and when I came back I wasn't really interested. It was one of the consequences of the war, and it was only to be expected. Also a consequence of the prevailing chaos. I also have information that the same thing went on, on the Muslim and Croat sides. Whoever was stronger took advantage. And there were paramilitary units on those sides as well, the Croat and Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, based on what I know from the positions you held in the Brcko municipality before the war and after the war, you were a man of considerable stature in the Brcko municipality. Are you saying that this extensive looting that resulted in Brcko being a devastated town, the rapes that are -- that Mr. Ristanic accounts for in this document, the unauthorised interrogations, the murders, the executions, was of no interest to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are two questions there, Your Honour. The first was a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we -- could we ask Mr. Harmon to split them up. Is that what you'd like in order to avoid any confusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, are you saying that the extensive looting that resulted in the devastation of the town of Brcko, the executions that are related in this, the rapes that are related in this report were of no interest to you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary. I was completely against it. I cannot tell you all of it in half a minute, but I can tell you about one episode when I almost lost my life because of all that. One column of fighters around the front line was looting TV sets and other things, and I came out in front of them. I told them, "This is not appropriate. This is not proper conduct." And their commander confronted me, took out his gun, and I saw that it was wiser to withdraw. There's no question of me approving of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely condemned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say you absolutely condemned it, what did you do to report those crimes to your higher authorities in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war broke out, I held no more positions, and it was not within my power to do anything. I was an invalid occupying no position of power whatsoever, and I was not placed to report it to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, you have told us earlier that you were a close associate of Dr. Beli. You held a responsible position in the SDS position. You held that position when you came back from your -- from your treatment in Belgrade. To whom did you report your concerns about the crimes that had taken place in Brcko of which you were aware and of which you apparently were almost a victim?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire leadership headed by Dr. Beli was, and this is something I learnt later on, because you have to know that all the improper conduct ended once I ended my treatment. However, in this time of prevailing chaos, any soldier carrying weapons capable of fighting was more important than Dr. Beli himself, and that is why they were unable to do anything about it. You yourself stated that once they had even occupied the ministry of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I'm looking at the clock. I'm also looking at the time I said you would have. Mr. Maricic, you did not answer the last question. You told us a lot of things. Should we understand that to be that because of the de facto situation in which, as you said, any soldier carrying weapons capable of fighting was more important than Dr. Beli himself that you did not report any of the crimes you saw, the looting you saw? Is that how I have to understand your answer? Because the question was to whom you reported having seen this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wouldn't put it that way, really, not any soldier but the soldier who was a bit deranged and who was crime-prone, that type of man, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, but the core of the question was whether you did report that, those looting -- that looting being committed. You gave us a lot of circumstances. Do I have to understand that under those circumstances you did not report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not occupy any position, but I'm certain that Dr. Beli himself reported on these matters to the higher-up leadership asking that they take certain measures on -- I'm sure he did it dozen -- dozens of times. And not only him but other members of the leadership as well. But this was simply something that was beyond them. You see, in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, there were these semi-norms that were in force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand how you describe the present situation -- the situation at that time. Again, you didn't answer the question. The question was whether you did report, but I take it then that you say, "I'm sure Dr. Beli himself reported." So he reported. Is there any document of such reporting, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether there is a document, but I don't think that all of these reports were relayed verbally. I'm sure there must be something in writing as well. But I wasn't placed to do that, and I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know. Mr. Harmon, could you please wrap up?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have one additional question, Witness. If you could turn to tab 18. This is P5269, tab 463. Witness, if you turn to the last page in the B/C/S version, the second bullet point down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if you turn to page 5, the penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You see page 6, Mr. Maricic, the second bullet point?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It appears a third of the way down the page. It says "Krajina special police with 45 men led by Zivojin Ivanovic, aka Crnogorac, is present in the area of Brcko. He has not placed himself under the command of the Brcko Brigade. He was allegedly sent by the RSUP." Do you know who this man -- did you know this man?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can assist you. If the usher -- I would be glad point out where it is to the usher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have the last page in front of you? Then it is the third paragraph starting with "Na podrucja." I may pronounce it wrongly, but ... You found it, Mr. Maricic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please read the paragraph, the three lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What can you tell me about Mr. Ivanovic? Did you know him and --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never seen the man, and I don't know anything about him. If he did come to Brcko, then this must have taken place before I returned from my treatment, because had he been coming to Brcko after I ended my treatment, I would have known. I only heard of his nickname, Crnogorac, from people in general, but I never met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've concluded my examination. Thank you very much, Mr. Maricic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Josse, any need to re-examine the witness? Perhaps before you do so I'll just confront the witness with one issue. Mr. Maricic, yesterday at the very end of this court session I asked you a few questions about whether names I mentioned were SDS members. Then when I came to the last name, that was Radoslav Bogicevic, you answered, and I understood that answer. At least it was on my screen at that moment that you said, "I think he joined later, and he was an SDS member." I then asked you what he joined, what he did join later, and you answered that he joined the SDS. Since I had some difficulties in finding the logic of this answer and since I did not exclude for the possibility that the translation that reached me at that time was not, for the full hundred per cent, correct, I asked the interpreters to listen again to your original words and to check the translation. This resulted in your first answer being, "I think he joined later, and he, too, was a member, although only on paper, not in fact." The further explanation you gave, translation was reviewed, and finally the -- it now reads: "I mean, he joined the SDS a bit later, because his brother was in the Socialist Party, and he became a senior manager later. So he joined the SDS in order to facilitate this." Mr. Maricic, I have some difficulties in logically understanding the line where it says, "I think he joined later, and he, too, was a member," to understand that as joining the SDS as a member. Now being -- having listened to what I just said, could you assist me in how I could understand this line to be joining the SDS rather than anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know myself how to clarify this further. Many people became members of different parties for their own personal interests. That was my opinion and still is, and I meant of course personal material interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that, but I'd like to focus on the first answer you gave where you said, "I think he joined later." When I put those questions to you, I listed persons who were appointed members of, I think it was called the War Presidency. Therefore, one might be inclined to understand the words, "I think he joined later," to understand that Mr. Bogicevic joined the War Presidency later. What would you say to those who would be inclined to understand your words in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He became manager of Interplet. That's a furniture manufacturing company. And in order to become one, he probably needed that sort of support I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that he was -- he did not later become a member, but if you read the line, "I think he joined later and he, too, was a member," then especially the word "too" make it not very logic -- logical to understand joining as joining the club of which he became a member. That's my logical problem with your answer. So I'm not putting in dispute the reason why he became an SDS member. I'm focusing on what Mr. - what was his name - Bogicevic joined according to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant to say was that he became a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That doesn't resolve the matter. Mr. Josse, any immediate for -- to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In your language, as these answers have been translated back to you, is there any ambiguity at all in your mind as to what you said at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I think, but I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, the learned Judge is suggesting to you, that the answer you gave yesterday, this has now been retranslated by the translation service, was in some way ambiguous and your use of the word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not saying this was ambiguous and that's not what I was suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To be quite honest, I thought not that it was ambiguous, but I was trying to find whether it could be explained in such a way that any ambiguity I had not yet found in those words would arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, being frank with the Court, I did not follow what Your Honour was driving at, at all, with respect, and I simply didn't understand the line of questioning at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Perhaps I'll be in a position to clarify this so that the Defence at least has the -- has the advantage of knowing what was, at least on my mind, not what I finally made up but what was on my mind when I put the questions to the witness and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think we'd be very grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move on then. Could I have one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to take you back, Mr. Maricic, to an assertion that Mr. Harmon made in his cross-examination today, which he then didn't turn into a question, and I would like you to deal with this, if you'd be so kind. Your Honour, this is page 18 at approximately line 22, 23. What was asserted, Mr. Maricic, was this: That based on information from the positions you held in the Brcko municipality before and after the war, you were a man of considerable stature in that municipality. What do you say about that assertion?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall what I stated, but if need be, I can reiterate that I was not in Brcko because of my positions there. My positions were of relative weight. I was known around Brcko because I went about the town and because I was part of the forces that defended the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you talking about before or after the war or both?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three periods, before the war, during the war, and after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you have P1124 in front of you again, please. That is the document dealing with this organisation, the combatants' -- I beg your pardon, Republican Association of Participants in the War since 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't think the usher can find the document, Your Honour. I need mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you're referring to the website page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does this organisation have anything to do with combatants who were involved in the Croatian war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. It is quite interesting that it says -- or, rather, that it's called "since -- in the war since 1990." I could not confirm or disprove your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other thing which may assist in this regard. Can you tell the Chamber when your military pension is dated from? I assume for the purpose of this question that you get a military pension.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not receiving a military pension but a civilian one, and it's a pittance, something that can't -- one can't live by, and I'm receiving an allowance on account of my military service, but that one is also a minimum one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when is the start date of your service deemed to be?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. You said in your evidence, in answer to a question that my learned friend asked you, that the JNA did cooperate with paramilitary units that had arrived in Brcko. Are you able to say why the JNA cooperated with those paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I stated was on the basis of what I heard from other people, but I also said that the JNA had the total of 100 men in Brcko prior to the war, and when the war broke out the numbers did not really increase. That's why the JNA did not have a decisive command role in the early days of the war in Brcko, rather, the command was held by those others that you mentioned and, of course, the manpower present in the barracks was compelled not only to cooperate with them but to execute their orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were asked about the Chetniks of a man - and I hope I pronounce this right - called Mihajlovic. Are those Chetniks, Mr. Mihajlovic's Chetniks, connected to Seselj's Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of the former Yugoslavia there are several Chetnik organisations. In my opinion, none of them has really anything to do with the -- the Chetniks of Draza Mihajlovic. In response to the Prosecutor's question, I said that I was a member of their party for a short while. As soon as I realised that those were not honourable men and their policies were not honourable, I quit. Draza Mihajlovic and his men were honourable fighters. I suppose that among those who now term themselves -- style themselves Chetniks, there are honourable men as well, but the ones that I met were not among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing else. Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Krajisnik is indicating to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take your time to consult with him if there's anything -- whether it's Mr. Krajisnik himself -- I think the procedure is, Mr. Krajisnik, that you consult with counsel and then put questions to the witness or instruct counsel to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, while those consultations are going on, I just would like to inform the Court I do have copies now of the decision that I mentioned at the beginning of the testimony, and I inform Mr. Maricic as well. So these could be entered into the record at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, from my own experience I know that it's very uncomfortable to have to consult in this way in the courtroom. If you'd need -- if you'd ask for a little bit -- a longer break so that you have a better opportunity to consult with Mr. Krajisnik, then I would allow that, even to suggest that if you need it that you ask for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Krajisnik and I would both appreciate that. It's a conceptual difficulty rather than a -- rather than a difference of opinion on our part. Let me -- I'm quite willing to ask the witness if I understand exactly what Mr. Krajisnik has in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that it took you more time, so therefore I guessed that it might be a little bit more complex matter than just, "Please put this question and that question to the witness." Then if we would take 35 minutes for a break, would that do?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That would do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then at the same time I would invite you to have a look at the last decision, conversion of couple of months of imprisonment to 4.500 marks because Mr. Harmon just announced that he could distribute them. So perhaps we could give him an opportunity to do so now and you can read that. Then I would like to know after the break whether you would oppose admitting this as an exhibit not introduced through a witness or whether you would like to put additional questions to the witness in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Could I mention one other thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do now have the document in relation to the detained witness in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to read that as well because I imagine that's an issue the Court will want to address this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's mainly -- I'd ask you whether the suggested course of -- course to take which might be videolink to consider that and to hear from you whether that would be an acceptable way of at least hearing the evidence of that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for forewarning me. I would like to speak to Mr. Stewart about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we take a bit more or -- yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Should this have a number at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think. Mr. Josse, I think it's -- to give it provisionally rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The chances of my opposing this would be extremely slim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be my guess as well. Mr. Registrar that would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1130, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, wouldn't it be best to have a break until 4.30 to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- have a little bit more time? Mr. Maricic, we will have a break. There may be some more questions for you after the break. We're not sure about it, but we'd like to see you back in 45 minutes. We will adjourn until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before we continue with the witness, there are a few procedural matters pending already for quite some time which I'd like to deal with. The first issue I'd like to address is the -- if I could call it interpretation incident in relation to Mr. Poplasen. This Trial Chamber would like to address the parties regarding an incident which occurred on the 10th of March. Witness Poplasen stated in the second session that he had heard an offensive comment during his testimony exclusively broadcasted on the B/C/S channel. The Chamber informed the witness that it would inquire into the matter. The Chamber has concluded, based on the inquiry and explanation made by the Conference And Language Services Section, that an offensive remark was made by one of the CLSS conference interpreters in the booth in reaction to a statement made by the witness in a video clip presented as evidence. The interpreter's remark was inadvertently broadcast on the B/C/S channel. The phrase used by the interpreter in question and heard by the a witness, and I quote "Jao sto sere." I would like to invite the interpreters to translate this phrase into English and French into order to record the translation of the original phrase in the transcript I just pronounced.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "He is full of shit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if it does not appear to the Chamber to arise from any ethnic prejudice or hostility to the Defence, the comment was entirely inappropriate. Such comments are not acceptable in this Chamber or at the Tribunal. The Chamber is satisfied that appropriate action has been taken in respect of the interpreter in question in order to prevent future incidents of this nature. Furthermore, this interpreter offered to be removed from this case. This interpreter will no longer be assigned to work on the Krajisnik trial. In addition, CLSS convened a staff meeting of all Tribunal conference interpreters to remind them their professional obligations under Article 4 of the Tribunal's Code of Ethics for Translators and Interpreters requiring interpreters to maintain a professional attitude in dealings with all persons inside the courtroom, including witnesses. All Tribunal conference interpreters have been instructed to refrain from making any comments in the interpretation booth. On behalf of the Tribunal, the Chamber would like to apologise to Witness Poplasen for the remark in question. It should not have occurred. The Chamber kindly requests the Registrar to inform the Victims and Witnesses Section of this statement and to convey the transcript of this statement to Mr. Poplasen. This concludes the Chamber's statement on this matter. I will now move to some exhibit issues. The exhibits introduced through Witness Poplasen, parties have been invited to consider will there are any objections. Could I hear from the Defence first. That's the document you had earlier not with you, Mr. Josse. It starts I think at P1074 and as far as Defence exhibits are concerned is starts with D142. If you're not prepared, then I hear from you after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would prefer that. I am very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, its-- can happen. Would the same be true for the Radojko exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got no observations about any of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then I think that since Mr. Tieger came for the Radojko exhibits, then at least I would invite him to express any -- of course, the problem would be that Mr. Tieger would like to be present if you raise any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I still -- I have none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have none? Then I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I said I have no observations. I occasionally use that word to mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That you're not entirely happy but that you leave it as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood you well. That is true for both Poplasen and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. No, I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Just Radojko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just Radojko. Okay. Then, Mr. Tieger, since you're here, and that was my concern at the moment, any objection to any exhibit introduced by the Defence through Witness Radojko?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then all exhibits tendered through the Witness Poplasen -- Mr. Radojko, that is for the Prosecution, that is P1098 up to and including P1108, are admitted into evidence. And as far as Defence exhibits are concerned, it is D145. They're admitted into evidence. Then Poplasen, I don't remember, was it you, Mr. Harmon, who will deal with Poplasen or -- yes. So then we'll hear then from Mr. Josse after the next break, and I expect you to be here, Mr. Tieger, at least -- I don't know if you need to stay for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, everything's going so well so far, Your Honour, I think I'll stick around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then there is another matter. We have some other issues about admission and the status of exhibits. I'd like to address you concerning your respective exhibits tendered during the recent examination of Witness Lakic. Several exhibits are ready to be admitted into evidence at this time. This includes, for the Prosecution, P1109 up to and including P1117, and for the Defence, D148. The Chamber asks the parties to submit all objections to these exhibits by Friday, that's tomorrow, 24th of March, otherwise they'll be automatically entered into evidence. The Defence also submitted several items that require translation, and that is D146, D147, and D149. The Chamber asks that all translations be completed by no later than the 10th of April, 2006. Additionally, the Chamber asks the Prosecution to report on their progress today or tomorrow in complying with the omnibus order of the 2nd of March. Pages 3 and 4 of the order stipulated that the Prosecution produce any documents surrounding the death of Husein Hotic in the Japra valley by the 16th of March. The Chamber has not yet received these materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can report now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Counsel and I were to meet at some point in time. I had submitted within a day or two of the omnibus order a list of proposed exhibits untranslated to the Defence. I have in the meantime had those documents translated and I'm prepared to submit them at any time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We asked you to submit them, so then we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will submit them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are we able to look at them before they're submitted, in translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm getting them as -- on a daily basis, Your Honour. Yes, I assume the Defence, when I identified the documents with their language assistants, would look over them themselves. I only started receiving these in the last couple days. I assume the Defence was completely familiar with the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine Mr. Josse wants to form an opinion on these documents and working late at night and perhaps not -- no one is available to translate for him the originals, that he'd like to have the English translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm more than happy to accommodate Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not matter which -- of course we asked for it and progress is now made as far as I understand and we'll prompt Mr. Josse just then to read them over so that if we'd ask whether there's any objection to them that he can answer that question from his own knowledge and not only secondhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the risk of being pedantic the order in relation to the Lakic exhibits is that objections in writing, and, if so, by what time, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you ask whether we do that at the end of the day, would I not object, but we're sitting tomorrow morning, from what I understand, and if you'd say I could do it, then -- but preferably then in writing by the very end of the day so not at the end of the session, then we'd consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I'm not going to be able to personally do it tomorrow morning because obviously I'm going to be in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Josse, if you have any alternative proposal. But I do understand that our proposal is not clear to you. But if you -- it seems that you might have some problems in --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ask what you'd like us to grant you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Monday morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then that's my next issue, that we will not sit Monday morning but we will sit in the afternoon, upon your request, as I understand. Then we make that even Monday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Your Honour in respect to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have checked -- at least, we have checked our agendas and I don't know if all technical matters have already been resolved but at least the Judges are willing to sit in the afternoon and I think that the Prosecution was consulted as well to move from Monday morning to afternoon. No problem. I have not verified myself whether all our support staff or whether that's all -- whether we did organise it all. I see Mr. Registrar is nodding yes, so a lot of efforts have already been made to make this move to the afternoon possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: On behalf of the Defence, might I say a collective thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that -- then you have time until Monday in the afternoon to -- to raise any objections in relation to the Lakic documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move on to the next issue, and that is that the Chamber also asks for a response today or tomorrow from the Defence, and I'm referring to transcript page 21.534, as they have yet to submit Exhibits D114. It was due on the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's going to be done now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's great. We asked for today or tomorrow, so even if you would have done it tomorrow, it would be -- but before members of the team move out, I have more on my list.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Chamber would like to remind the Defence that it was also asked, and now I'm referring to transcript page 21.053, to produce the list of criminal cases from Kotor Varos municipality referenced in the testimony of Witness D14 by Friday, the 24th of March. The Chamber also expects the Defence to submit D123 and D139 by next Monday, the 27th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for reminding me about the D14 issue. That is one I will pursue when the Court rises today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then now to keep everything in balance, the Prosecution, and I now refer to page 3 of the 2nd of March omnibus order was to submit the contracts and material supporting exhibit P340 to both the Chamber and the Defence by the 16th of March. The Prosecution was granted an extension until the 30th of March, and the Chamber kindly reminds you that it awaits those materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I may comment, Your Honour. I'm aware of the deadline. I received your report from the field yesterday evening. I have a report. I need to study the report. I have been informed that there are possibly some obstructions in respect of that. I haven't studied it. It was an oral report to me from the field. I need to look at it and I'll keep the Chamber advised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber also recalls that it addressed the parties on the 9th of March at transcript page 21.050 and 51 and asked them to agree upon the type and amount of materials to submitted to the Chamber regarding the legal decisions of Bosnian courts that may help shed light on circumstances in Bosanski Novi. These materials are to be submitted by today, 23rd of March. In the alternative, both parties are expected to make oral or written submissions. Was any agreement reached?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The answer is no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that due to fierce disagreement or it's by just lack of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think it's lack of time, Your Honour. We have some materials we provided those to the Defence a while ago. I've not had the opportunity to engage in discussions after the Defence has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- looked at those materials, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the parties prefer to have an extension of time or would they rather say well, let's already make oral or written submissions? I think it makes sense to ask for an extension of time, but I'm not dictating what you should ask for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm perfectly satisfied to do that. We will be ready, Your Honour, on that issue. It's a question of the Defence having the opportunity to look at those again and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, how much time do you think you need to reach an agreement or to decide that you have no agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, realistically at least another week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: New date is set for the 30th of March. Finally, the parties were asked on the 10th of March, transcript page 21.065, to agree upon the necessity of translating the spoken commentary in the video concerning the attack on a convoy in Tuzla. The Defence took it upon itself to decide whether a translation was necessary. We would like you to ask -- to respond by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, the answer to that is resources dictate that there will be no transcript provided, and the Chamber will need to view the video silently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This then concludes my questions and my statement of the -- on the admission and the status of exhibits, but, Mr. Harmon, you have another matter to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have two matters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One, I am informed that Prosecution Exhibit 583 tab 7 needed a corrected translation. I have that corrected translation now which I can furnish to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The second issue deals with a witness who is to be called on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We received, as Your Honour is aware, late notice of the witness. I am concerned about our ability to be ready, frankly, by Monday on this particular witness. We have gone through a series of quick changes for reasons that are known to the Court. I make no comments on that, but it has put us at a serious disadvantage as to our preparation time. As the Court knows, we make every effort to accommodate the Court and the Defence in this respect, but I would like to foreshadow the difficulties that I can see coming with the witness who was scheduled for Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber also regrets that the Defence fails repeatedly to give in due time the information the Prosecution needs to cross-examine witnesses. Even if no drastic measures are taken now, immediately, it does not mean that it is a kind of silent acceptance by the Chamber of this practice. Unless there's really something important to say about it, Mr. Josse, I would like to leave it to that at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is nothing important to say other than there is no more information that we can provide in relation to this witness at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Of course, you're expected to get your information so timely that you would be in a position to do that, but let's not restart this discussion at this moment. It will not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the whys and wherefors of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The whys and wherefors of that is, as Your Honour knows, a complicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- convoluted and protracted matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes I am aware of that and at the same time I am aware that the Chamber gave some decisions and orders in this respected which are not consistently followed. As I said, I'd like to leave it to that at this very moment. Mr. Harmon, you have provided us with a P1130 just before the break. There are a few matters. First of all, the translation says that a fee was imposed, where I take it that "the fine" is the proper translation. It appears twice. You first find it in the middle of page 1, "hereby commuted to a fee," which should be a fine. And I take it that the translation was made in -- very quickly and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second page, the word "fee" appears again, and just a few lines before the signature of the judge and the notary we find "500 convertible marks." It should be 50. First of all, the original says 50; and secondly, 50 is the amount mentioned in Article 37, paragraph 2 of the Republika Srpska Criminal Code. So it's both for legal regions. I also just note at this moment, Mr. Josse, that apart from reference to these articles of the Republika Srpska Criminal Code, which mainly say that it is possible upon the request of someone sentenced to convert a prison sentence of not more than three months into a fine and Article 37 allowing to -- well, several systems of payment, that therefore I have no substantive reasons apart from THAT this is legally possible upon the request of the accused. Since the witness will leave and since we do not establish facts but I would say the old Latin saying is jus curia novit, the court knows the law, it's a matter of law, I think I could bring to your attention apart from any substantial reasons, specific reasons for this case that the reference is mainly to the legal possibility to do this. And I take it the decision doesn't say who can appeal against this decision but it's a final decision by now. I would not expect the witness to appeal this decision since he requested it to be taken. That's what I had on my mind. Perhaps, Mr. Harmon, it would be good to have a full, correct translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll submit that tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got one matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Defence filed on the 17th of March a request for clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- in relation to a certain matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A response to that is -- or is not going to be forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're still considering the matter, whether and, if so, what clarification the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are a lot of questions in --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll be told if no clarification is going to be forthcoming, presumably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if finally -- we don't let you wait for months and months and then to find out that the Chamber is not intending to give any clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once we've made up our mind we'll let you know. If the clarification is there if you hear about it; if no clarification will be there we'll inform you about it, that no clarification will be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further procedural issue? Then I think we could -- yes. Mr. Josse, the long break was to enable you to consult with Mr. Krajisnik. Are there any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are three or four topics he wants me to re-examine upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All of them do arise from cross-examination, I can say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. And, Mr. Josse, once he's in, you may start your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, notwithstanding Your Honour's comments about the 1130, I would rather show it to the witness if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No problem. I just thought that it might assist the parties. You may not have found time immediately to verify the articles mentioned in it, to give at least an impression of what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Maricic. Mr. Josse has a few more questions for you. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Maricic be given a copy of P1130.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This, Mr. Maricic, is the document that was mentioned to you at the beginning of today, document which has been obtained overnight, which shows that your sentence of imprisonment was commuted to a fine of 4.500 convertible -- 4.500 convertible marks. Have you seen this particular document before?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this document. I received this document perhaps within ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is a suggestion that the sentence was altered or commuted from imprisonment to a fine as a result of your invoking a statutory provision in the Republika Srpska Criminal Code which allows persons who are sentenced to three months or less imprisonment to pay a fine instead. Can you comment upon that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done by my lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I suggested that it was possible to make a request to that extent, which allows persons who are sentenced to -- less to pay a fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We now know the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was just keen to clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And some might say slightly bizarrely this notice says that an appeal can be filed against this decision, presumably by the accused rather than the prosecution. You obviously did not appeal this decision which bearing in mind what had happened you were content with, you having elected to pay the fine rather than going to prison. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to return to the issue of the document P1124. And I was asking you earlier some questions in relation to your war service. Are you able to tell the Chamber from your own personal knowledge from what date is your status as a combatant in the war deemed to start from?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think from the date I went to the front line, which I believe was the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Such pension rights as you've got, are they affected by the fact that you were invalided out of the war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you receive any pension for having been a combatant, in fact?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've stated that I have been receiving a minimum civilian pension, no other. I have also been receiving a minimum sum of an allowance as a war invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just explain about what being a war invalid means. It maybe obvious, but it would help if you put that some other way if you could.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wounded on -- at the front line in combat. Any such persons, if invalided based on the findings of a medical commission are granted the status of war invalids.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you turn, please, to tab 18. If we look at the very end of this document dated the 13th of August of 1992, like I said, we see that it is dated the 13th of August, 1992. It's addressed to the president of SRBH Presidency, the prime minister, and the army Main Staff commander. Could you have a look, please, at the last paragraph of the first page. It's the last paragraph of the first page in English as well, helpfully. It says: "None of the paramilitary formations expresses political affiliation to the ruling SDS. On the contrary, all have political ties with the opposition parties from Serbia, the SPO, the Serbian renewal movements, SNO, SRS," and so on. Are you able to comment on that paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that states rightly that most of them did not declare themselves to be members of the SDS. I know what these abbreviations mean. However, the Socialist Party of Serbia and JUL should be added to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've obviously got no idea what the president of the Presidency did if and when he received this document?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 17, please. You've been taken to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
