utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just to interrupt. So the record is perfectly clear, I think it's important the exhibit number is posted as opposed to the tab number being inserted into the record, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, except 18 might be difficult to retrieve, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can help for the purposes of the last exhibit refers to is P529, tab 463, and the exhibit, then, tab 17, is Prosecution Exhibit 529, Hanson tab 74.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You've been taken to parts of this summary of events and situations with an assessment of the degree of achievement which appears to be undated and purports to be signed by the War Presidency of Brcko municipality. The last paragraph of the report or the summary says: "The goal of this analysis of the situation so far is to direct attention to the results achieved and current problems that must be resolved as soon as possible. All other necessary information available to us will be presented in a more detailed conversation with the senior organs." Do you have any idea for whose benefit or purpose this document was composed?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I can't say who composed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The last paragraph that I have just read out to you, could you explain that in some other words? What is the author of this driving at?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I object to that. That calls for an interpretation that this witness, I don't think, is able to give or should be permitted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't know yet, Mr. Harmon, whether he is able witness is able so the witness is allowed to answer the question it could be that he has some special knowledge that would clarify but let's wait and see what he says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean the last paragraph on this first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I beg your pardon. The last paragraph that I read out on the very last page. You're going the wrong way, Mr. Maricic. It's -- it's a difficult document, I know, because it's got these stamps from a Tribunal official interspersed on every other page. So, Madam Usher, the last paragraph on the last page immediately above the signature.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on this. It is quite vague. I don't know even when it was written. The conclusion that I can draw from this is that this serves to draw attention to problems arising from poor coordination and the fact that many units were out of anyone's control.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions either. Mr. Maricic, this concludes your testimony in this court. You've answered questions of both parties and questions put to you by the Bench. I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Maricic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we have some time left to the break, could we deal with the exhibits introduced through Mr. Maricic. Mr. Registrar, that would be from.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P118, Your Honours, up until P1130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D150 up until and including D152.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are the parties in a position to immediately address any objections they'd like to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If Your Honour would literally give me a moment, perhaps I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we could also do is to have the break now and do this immediately after the break, and then we'll hear any report on the Poplasen exhibits as well. You also received the list from Mr. Registrar of all the exhibits listed which were introduced through Mr. Maricic. Then we could both deal with the Poplasen, and if you would need more time for the exhibits introduced through Mr. Maricic, please ask for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. On this occasion I think I'd be quite keen to deal with it after a short break while it's fresh in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Perhaps I -- then perhaps use the time to the extent that you're in a position to respond to the issue addressed in the memo by the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I have spoken to Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have -- of course, he hasn't read this document, and I'm bound to say in an ideal world I would like him to do that. But I also made this observation: I noticed that the letter from the chief court management at the registry of the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina was obviously written in B/C/S. We don't have the original of that letter, and I'd very much like my client to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I did telephone the person to whom it's addressed at the VWS and left her a message. She wasn't at her desk. I've been in court since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm prepared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you want to verify everything. Mr. Josse, let me add to this that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the Defence was very late with asking the Chamber to take action in order to make sure that Mr. Bjelica would appear in this courtroom. Now -- it turns out now what consequences this has, because we are again fighting against time because if finally there would be no possibility to have Mr. Bjelica here in court preparing for videolink takes time as well. So I'm -- I just want to urge the Defence to make up its mind as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make some submissions now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The reason I have a preamble --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- is before any final decision is made, I would urge the Chamber to reflect some sure at will on what I say. No doubt there may be some feedback and I could then speak to Mr. Stewart overnight and with a bit of luck Mr. Krajisnik may get a copy of this letter. But, Your Honour, I can assist because, as I've already indicated, most of the issues dealt with in this letter were stated to us at a meeting Mr. Stewart and I attended two or three nights ago. The problem with a videolink is really two or threefold. I understand there are problems, logistical problems from the Registry and Chamber's point of view. But so far as of the Defence is concerned it will either realistically means that either Mr. Stewart or I would need to spend four days in the Republika Srpska. This man has been seen by me for approximately an hour when he had his liberty. It was a long time ago. He gave me a very large number of documents, most of which have been looked at by members of our team, some of which - not many, I'm bound to say - have been translated and are going to be used, but there are a lot of documents. He's also produced a video that we were intending to play, at least in part. His evidence is relatively complicated, and we submit of some real importance. He requires approximately two days' proving by any stretch of the imagination. Two days proofing, respectively, two days travelling. One of us would have to spend four days in the Republika Srpska. It's really as simple as that as far as we can see. Second drawback, of course, is it means the witness wouldn't be able to see our client in the normal way of things. I appreciate -- Mr. Krajisnik may not entirely agree with this but I appreciate that bearing in mind the very unusual circumstances, that may not be a consideration in the forefront of the mind of the Chamber. So, Your Honour, there are serious practical difficulties as far as we are concerned. Finally and the third point is I am also painfully aware that if he's going to be called, he needs to be called sooner rather than later. Let's leave aside the schedule that we're under, and I'm not diminishing that for one moment, but we can put it aside for the purpose of this submission. Clearly he needs to leave the Republika Srpska if he's going to leave the Republika Srpska again sooner rather than later. His trial is going to begin in due course, and were he to give evidence -- were he to be required to give evidence sometime in the future in The Hague, then it's going to be very much harder to bring him here. Common sense dictates that. A member of our team spoke yesterday to his lawyer who, broadly speaking said, as far as he the lawyer was concerned the witness was available to come to The Hague forthwith so far as his case in Bosnia is concerned, if Your Honour sees what I mean by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider what you've said. At the same time, I think that everyone should understood the efforts made by the Chamber until now, and now again urging you as quickly as possible make up your mind on what course we should take in this respect. It is because the Chamber is very much concerned not to lose any evidence that might be of importance for the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Our position is plain and simple. We want him brought here as soon as possible. There's absolutely no ambiguity about that whatsoever. I -- in the course of the submissions I have just made, I was trying to be realistic about the problems that everyone in this courtroom faces, those in Bosnia face, but our position is plain: We want the 90 bis order executed as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question is whether that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And whether it's not possible whether a second-best solution, whether we should start preparing it. That's the issue. Of course, I do understand that you'd like to have the witness here. Of course, it would have been better to apply for such an order far earlier and to do it at a moment when there was still some flexibility, because the present scheduling tells you that by the 4th of April your case presentation -- the presentation of the evidence -- of the witnesses before Mr. Krajisnik's testimony would -- would have to -- to finish, unless you would have to -- unless you would have decided. Then we alluded to that a couple of days earlier to -- well, say, to sacrifice some of the time you intended to spend on the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik for other witnesses. I fully understand what you would like to happen. The question is that how realistic it is at this moment that it could happen as you wish it to happen, and second, what alternatives there. I'm not saying you should give up, but one thing is for sure, that the alternative of a videolink is not seriously considered at this moment we might end up in a situation that neither the presence of the witness here could be achieved nor a videolink in due time. So therefore that's, I think, the problem we'll -- yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One comment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One comment to make to the Court in respect of what Mr. Josse has just said. He says that he has identified -- Mr. Bjelica gave the Defence a significant number of documents, some of which have been identified and is -- for use in the testimony of Mr. Bjelica, and in respect of the order of this Court to provide to the parties 14 days in advance exhibits, we would therefore request now copies of those exhibits to be provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse. Of course, the exhibit list under 65 ter is not complete, but Mr. Harmon says you received documents. You want to use them. Part of them are even already translated from what I understand. Mr. Harmon would like to receive them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll ask that that be arranged. It's a reasonable request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- and I will ask that someone in our team attend to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break until five minutes to six. We'll then first deal with any objections, Poplasen and Mr. Maricic, and then are you ready to call your next witness, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I -- I am. I wouldn't mind going to see him for five minutes simply because I told him he was going to be on about two and a half hours ago. That's my fault, not his, but I think it might only be fair that I reassure him because I suspect he's been sitting in this building for the last four hours or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think 20 minutes should be enough to do that. We'll adjourn until five minutes to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I do understand that you have been provided with an English translation of the letter on the what you call the Bjelica issue and that a B/C/S version is available now as well. Then I'd like to ask you the following, to consider, because we have given it quite some attention also during this break, if for whatever reasons the Chamber would consider it fair to grant two or three or four extra days so that you would not have to finish the presentation of witnesses on the 4th of April but, let's say, the 5th or the 6th or the 7th, and if we would be able to get Mr. Bjelica here in, well, let's say approximately 10 days, which would mean arrival the 3rd or the 4th, would you consider to -- then to take all the risks that other witnesses that are here, you have to finish them quickly, you have to -- if they come late or if they are -- have the flu or whatever then it would be Mr. Bjelica. You have to prioritise what's most important for you because if we would -- if we would take this course, if it's possible at all, if we would grant it, if it's possible for VWS, if -- well, let's say, technical difficulties such as documents which are needed and are not found yet although the existence is -- travel documents, for example, that the existence is not in dispute, I'd like you to consider whether or not you find Mr. Bjelica to be in court here so important that if this opportunity would be given whether you would take that with both hands and give it full priority or not, because it takes a huge effort from everyone. It also takes, again, the effort for the Chamber. I mean, even we, we're human beings as well, we are not able to schedule anything for ourselves any more apart from taking off weeks, which is usual in this Tribunal in spring. We don't do that. But then, of course, a full commitment to start tomorrow morning, so you have one night to consider that and to speak about it with Mr. Stewart, if he comes in court tomorrow morning, then the less time it takes the better it is if you would go out five minutes past nine or ten minutes past nine to start further preparing everything it's better than 9.30. That's what I put to you, something to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly what we'll do. We'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you need any further guidance, you can get in touch with the legal staff of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They've been very helpful in this regard hitherto, I might add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because as a matter of fact, half an hour ago I would have considered it totally impossible to have Mr. Bjelica here before the start of the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik at all, and I had serious doubts on whether it would be possible at all to have a video -- videolink there, and I was of course also very much concerned about taking time off from the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik. But this is to be considered. If you need any further information, please address Mr. Zahar. Any further matter at this moment? I don't think there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can deal with these exhibits as and when the Chamber requires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do it as quickly as possible. We had on our list Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as Mr. Poplasen is concerned, the only objection is to P1078. That's found at tab 6 in the bundle of documents. It is the -- described the partial translation from Glas Srpski dated August 1993, highly prejudicial. Derogatory assertions which he completely denied. Bearing in mind he completely denied it, in our submission it could have no evidential value whatsoever. It's worse than hearsay; it's bit of journalistic rubbish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we seek its admission, this is a document that Mr. Poplasen claimed was a forgery. This is a document which comes from Glas Srpski which is the -- the Court has heard the status of that particular newspaper. We believe it is admissible. It goes to his credibility, and it should be admitted, in our view. There are similar statements made by Mr. Poplasen of a similar nature. If I turn to the document that's in tab 8, Mr. Poplasen didn't dispute the fact that he called for retaliation against UN -- UNPROFOR forces. This is from a journal that is an official organ or official newspaper of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I know Mr. Harmon doesn't mean that but that is disingenuous to draw an analogy between what Poplasen said in tab 8 to what he says at tab 7, allegedly, where he uses the word physically liquidate members of UNPROFOR. The analogy simply is not fair nor accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider the matter. Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Poplasen. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no objections --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no objection to the exhibits, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Then the exhibits tendered through Mr. Maricic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as Mr. Maricic is concerned, Your Honour, tab 31, P1118 is objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the Tanjug article.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Again it's a newspaper article. The short bit that was in effect put to him where it -- the article which, by the way, is not altogether clear what this piece of paper is, although I dare say Mr. Harmon can help as far as that is concerned, it's not a newspaper article as such, whether it's come off the internet, I don't know. I assume it has, bearing in mind what appears at the bottom of the piece of paper, but it's the penultimate paragraph which the Prosecution relied upon where it alleged that the witness was first commander of the Serb Territorial Defence of Brcko to be acting chief, really, very similar point. No source, appears on the internet. The Chamber can't place any reliance upon it whatsoever. If this is the best Prosecution can do, well, I need not say any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever our decision may be, but first, Mr. Harmon, I give you an opportunity to respond, but at least what it refers to should be stricken from the reference to what the exhibit is because it's comment rather than identification of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's our position and our submission that Mr. Maricic was the first commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence in Brcko. It is our position that his denial was untruthful. This is a document that asserts that, and it's our view that this is admissible and the Court can consider this document when considering the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not a full answer to what Mr. Josse raised, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, if my learned friend wants to call this a document, then his definition and mine differs, but it's for Your Honours to decide, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider the matter. Any other objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Transport of munition authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'll withdraw my objection in relation to that document. That concludes my submission in relation to Mr. Maricic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections against Defence exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then all the exhibits which were not objected to are admitted into evidence and the Chamber will decide in due course on the -- on -- it was P1118. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll excuse myself at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krsman. At least I take it you're Mr. Krsman. Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsman. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Josse, counsel for the Defence. Mr. Josse, from the 65 ter summary I saw that -- I don't know how much time you're going to spend on it and how general or how specific it will be, but one of these days you heard from Mr. Harmon, and I take it Mr. Tieger takes the same position, that a lot of facts which may have some relevance for sentencing are not disputed by the Prosecution. I'm mainly talking about attacks from other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have a submission to make about that. Is Your Honour referring to the last paragraph of the penultimate page of the 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- I'm -- no. I think -- I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm -- I'm referring to the 7th of February, 2006, but it might be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My fault. I was looking at a different document, more an expansive one that I have in my papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether we --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've now got the 65 ter in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And something about crimes committed against -- well, you may have noticed --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: On the last page. The top of the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's put as part of another document I have in front of me, so it was very short at that time, isn't it, the 65 ter summary of the 7th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Oh, I don't even have that because it's been significantly expanded since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not spend too much time on it. I'll further look at it. But since it reads there "and the crimes committed against Serb population by the Muslims," that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, we have a submission about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I -- probably needs to be done in the witness's absence. Tomorrow morning would be fine. I'm not going to get to it until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please start your examination. I think I'm referring to the 7th of February, because we never received another one as far as I understand. So if at least you'd send it by e-mail later today so we can look at it over night.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Can I check that Mr. Tieger's got it. 18th -- it's actually stating on the top of it, 18th of March, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then Mr. Tieger has it. We have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And does the Chamber need it, bearing in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, 65 ter summaries are there to be produced at the beginning of the Defence case and to be presented to the Chamber and of course Mr. Tieger has a copy as well, but primary purpose is for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Primary purpose. Sorry, I hadn't appreciated that -- the import of the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that we can decide on issues, on how much time would be needed, what scheduling, et cetera. It's exactly the issue which has come up again and again and again that this Chamber is not in the position to schedule, to adapt schedules, to take into consideration changing situations since it has not been provided with the basic information it needs to -- not to conduct the trial because the parties will present the evidence. But the Chamber is responsible for scheduling, the Chamber is responsible for granting time, and is not in a position to do that. So therefore, if I say 65 ter, if you read it, I think it doesn't say that the other party should be provided with it but that the Pre-Trial Judge should be provided with this information. Please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your name is Sinisa Krsman?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: No, my name is Sinisa Krsman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have given evidence in this building once before, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You gave evidence in the trial of Galic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I was a Defence witness in the case against General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as your background is concerned, you are from Rajlovac, where you grew up? That's where you lived till the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in Sarajevo, Rajlovac, the village of Zabrdje. That's where we lived until the war broke out, and then we became refugees, and we never returned there because everything is burnt down and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You did your military service in the JNA. You then began a university economics degree, but you gave that up and became a businessman.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I finished serving in 1980. After that I started to work and continued to work until the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll talk about -- or I'll asking you about that work in a few moments' time. You spent the war as a soldier and a company commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the war, I was in my village of Zabrdje first as commander of a squad then commander of a company until the Dayton Accords were signed and the war was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You then went to live in Lukavica where you now run a cafe?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Just after the signing of the Dayton Accords I moved to Lukavica and lived as a tenant in an apartment until I found a job that could provide me with a livelihood sufficient to keep me and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as politics is concerned, you were president of a youth organisation in the former Yugoslavia. What was the name of that organisation, please?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: That organisation was called the alliance of the socialist youth of the SFRY. It was only one form of political organisation, but the most important form was the Socialist Alliance of the Working People that consisted mainly of older people. We, the youth, engaged mainly in organising all sorts of excursions, day trips, various events.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were a member of the League of Communists realigned to your position within the youth organisation that you have just described. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: I was automatically admitted into the League of Communists, because a non-member of the League of Communists could not be the president of the youth organisation. However, I was replaced very quickly and expelled from the League of Communists, but I remained president of the youth organisation because I was widely respected and even loved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you did not join another political party till after the war when you joined the Serb Radical Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes, just after the Dayton Accords I became a member of the Serbian Radical Party because I believe that everybody has the right to choose the option that best represents himself and his goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have known Momcilo Krajisnik since you were a boy?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I've known him and his family, because both our families have been natives of Zabrdje for 4 or 500 years, and everybody knows one another in Zabrdje, and I knew Mr. Krajisnik especially closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, in 1988 [Realtime transcript read in error "1988"], you were working for an organisation called Slateks, which was a textile company; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The management of that company was in Banja Luka, and there was a branch company in Sarajevo, and I became chief of that branch company in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript says perhaps I said it 1998, but in fact it was 1988 that you got this job, just to clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You worked at that time from an office that was located in the home of Mr. Krajisnik. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes. This was not merely an office. It -- there were several office premises and warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where did Mr. -- or where were Mr. Krajisnik and his family's living quarters in relation to your office?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik resided with his family upstairs. His father, mother, and brother lived in an old house some 50 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For what are period of time did your office, the office of Slateks, remain in Mr. Krajisnik's home?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: I worked there for about one year, and after that I took up another position I believe the office premises stayed there for some five or six months more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the time that you were -- that you had your office in his home, what was Mr. Krajisnik's level of political interest and involvement as far as you could gauge?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik's level of participation was exclusively at the local level in that period of time, as was ours, in fact. We were preoccupied with basic problems such as water supply, transportation of pupils and so on and so forth. These were matters that were of great importance to us, and we were unable to find adequate solutions for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you left Slateks, what work did you then move into?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: I opened up a private business of my own and a shop at Zabrdje where I worked until the outbreak of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to hand out a map. Your Honour, there are various maps that we have got. I'm grateful to the Prosecution providing this one. It will certainly do for now. Maybe I'll present another map to the witness in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With the pointer, show the learned Judges where Zabrdje is, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It looks a bit repetitious, Mr. Josse. I think we had Zabrdje already several times under our eyes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I suspect I can lead on this therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This was a village that was almost exclusively occupied by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Not almost exclusively but, rather, there was only one house inhabited by Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And Rajlovac was in effect a collection of 11 villages on the outskirts of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. As you can see on this map, out of the 11 villages, 10 were purely Serb villages. There was only one mixed village, that's to say there were Serbs and Muslims. The map you see now, it says Matusi [phoen], Bjelice, Miljatovici, Lemezi. This map must be some 30 years old because these are old Serb families. Where it says Sokolje you can see there's not a single house here. This is very important for the Trial Chamber to know. Where none of the houses were marked on the map between 1972 and 1982, this was -- or, rather, 1992, according to the 1991 census some 20.000 Muslims settled the area. In the municipality of Rajlovac, you had the barracks and other companies which were all built on the Serbian land taken from the inhabitants of Zabrdje and other villages. That's to say that in the 20 years the make-up of our municipality had completely changed which led to the problems I mentioned in my earlier evidence when I said we were faced with various problems which we were unable to solve.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you have described how the municipality or the area had changed. It's also right that there was a Rajlovac municipality, but after Second World War it became part of the of the Novi Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 1991, early 1992, you described already the demography of the area. Were there any ethnic tensions apparent in Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: You see, the first and foremost problems we were faced with were those which dealt with food, and this was brought on by immigration. Initially we had sufficient water supplies; however, by the sudden influx of population of some 20.000 people, the water pressure was too low and we didn't have enough water. Secondly, public transportation became a problem. With the great influx of people, the public transportation became inadequate and people were late to work and pupils were late to school. Thirdly, in the area of employment, there were great difficulties, and we had to start defending our interests. To tell you the truth, we have to say that we didn't have any inter-ethnic problems, conflicts, or resentment. What we wanted was to start solving our problems in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were there any events which you would describe or perhaps I should say events or actions which you would describe as provocations by your neighbours from other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Up until March 1992, there had been no provocations along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A decision was made to separate again the Rajlovac municipality. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In the second half of 1991, we embarked on a legislative procedure with a view to establishing the municipality of Rajlovac. It was only on the 23rd of February, if I remember well, that we held a constituent session at which we set up the municipality of Rajlovac or, rather, reinstituted the municipality of Rajlovac, which had existed before World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At that time, the time of the reinstitution of the municipality of Rajlovac, were you involved in municipal politics or municipal affairs?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: I took part in that process as did any resident of Zabrdje and the area of Rajlovac. We endorsed the initiative with the support of very strong arguments that Muslims and Croats from the municipality of Novi Grad refused to accept. I must say that we were among the last ones to have set up this municipality and proclaimed it the Serb municipality of Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What part did you take, Mr. Krsman?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: The municipality of Rajlovac, as I've just said, comprises 11 villages and hamlets of the former municipality of Novi Grad wherein 95 per cent of the population were Serbs. Others were also given the possibility to declare through a referendum or otherwise whether they wished to continue living in the municipality of Rajlovac, and I believe that this was a correct and fair gesture on our part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. The last two questions I have asked perhaps you slightly misunderstood them, but you haven't exactly answered. My first question was whether you were involved in municipal politics as such at the time of the reinstitution of the Rajlovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: No. I wasn't politically active. I was a representative there on behalf of the youth organisation to see how far the initiative would go and the progress it made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing this that mind, what you have just said, what part did you take in the decision to form or reinstitute the old municipality?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: My participation was not significant, but I was present at the Assembly where this took place. There were legally elected representatives of the Assembly who proclaimed it at this particular session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What effect on the life of the citizens of Zabrdje was there as a result of the formation of the new municipality?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: You must know that this took place on the 23rd of February, 1992. Had there not been a war, we would have been one of the wealthiest municipalities in the former Yugoslavia for sure. However, the start of the war and hostilities forced us to spend the entire war on the front line and in combat. The only thing we experienced were the horrors of war because of the proximity of the line of separation. After the Dayton Accords, the Rajlovac municipality wanted to remain such as it was. However, the war led the events in a totally different direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We can see on the map the barracks that dominate this particular piece of paper; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Air force and technical school centre was the largest centre of the sort in the former Yugoslavia where cadets underwent training, as did the senior officers. Thousands of highly educated servicemen graduated from this centre and spent their entire service in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The occupants of the barracks moved out sometime in March. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: There's nothing to understand there. I know that. There were 10.000 cadets in the barracks. That's to say young persons up to 18 years of age. Already in March they were moving out because there was strong pressure exerted by their parents. They -- these cadets came from all over Yugoslavia. They moved out in March, and only officers who taught them remained in the barracks. These were teachers holding high ranks, lieutenant colonels, colonels, and of course the security of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What happened to the firearms that were contained within the arsenal of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: I must stress before the Trial Chamber another matter that is very important. Those of us who lived quite close to the barracks in these past 30 years that I've been living in Rajlovac, we entered only once into the barracks, because before that we had never entered the barracks to see what sort of weapons there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question. The question was what happened to the firearms that were contained within the arsenal of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That may be the problem with a leading question. I'm not criticising Mr. Josse. I understand why he's doing that. It sounded to me like the witness was trying to explain his knowledge of whatever arsenal existed beforehand or whatever weapons existed which, presumably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He started saying that he must stress another matter that's very important so that -- and then -- okay. If your -- the beginning of your answer would lead you shortly to answering the question, I'll allow you to proceed. I just want to draw your attention that finally we'd like to know what happened with the firearms. Please proceed, Mr. Krsman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the barracks there were very small amounts of weapons. These were an -- air defence weapons because this is an air force pilots and flight engineering centre. They had mortars and light cannons. None of the cannons we found there were over 40 millimetres in calibre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what happened to them, because that was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you now all the weapons left behind in the barracks, the ones that we came across. There were no other weapons. They had none. But we found that out only when we entered the barracks. I was just telling you that we had never enter the barracks before and didn't know how many weapons there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, ironically the difficulty may be that I'm not leading enough. Perhaps not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see what happens if you lead more. You're not blamed for the level of leading one minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your evidence is that Serbs enter the barracks and took some firearms and then Muslims entered the barracks and took some firearms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that Mr. Tieger here --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is a leading question, Your Honour, and I was then going to ask the witness to give some details, but he's going to give this evidence. If my learned friend is unhappy, then I'll simply deal with what happens next, what happens next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, you said you never entered the barracks before the war and that you didn't know how many weapons there were. Even without knowing how many there were, do you know what happened to the weapons that were there before the war? Have you any information about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information I have dates from the period when the JNA left the barracks and we as the TO took control of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And are you aware of -- did you have any reason when you took over -- did you have any reason to consider whether the weaponry left in the barracks which you found was the complete set of -- of weapons or whether there were any parts missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two months before entering the barracks, in agreement with our Muslim neighbours, that's to say pursuant an agreement between our Crisis Staff and theirs, we, the Serbs from my village, entered the barracks and took 202 pieces of weapons with 150 rounds of ammunition. We listed whatever we took on a piece of paper. On the same day, the Muslims from Sokolje came to the barracks after us and took 800 pieces of light weapons and 150 combat sets. They took the same uniforms as we did. We did not know what sort of weaponry there was in the barracks before the JNA retreated. We took the went months month of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You made a distinction between the weapons taken by the Muslims in -- where you called them 800 pieces of light weapons. The weapons you took, the 202 pieces, were those light weapons or any other weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the same. We took 200 pieces of light weapons, and they took 800 because there were many more of them. There were more able-bodied men since there were 10.000 people in that area, and we all took weapons against a receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How was the collection -- let me start again. As far as you were concerned, was this an agreement on your part, that is the Serbs' part, and the Muslims' part?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes. This was an agreement that we implemented, and the weapons were given to us by Colonel Miletic who was still at the barracks at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters -- interpreter adds the witness said: A commander of the barracks, Colonel Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, if this is a convenient moment to stop, then we'll continue tomorrow morning. Mr. Krsman, we'll stop for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. Mr. Josse, if it would be possible to send us the 65 ter summary as soon as possible, that would prevent us from having to come back to the Tribunal this evening and to fetch it. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
